title: Easy to use Template for Software Requirements Specification

sections.title: Easy to use Template for Software Requirements Specification
sections.text_preview: Start with a descriptive and succinct name for your project. Change the above with the name of your project.

sections.title: Purpose
sections.text_preview: Set the expectation for the product you’re building. So, start by defining the purpose of your product.

sections.title: Scope
sections.text_preview: Describe the software being specified. Include benefits, objectives, and goals. This should relate to overall business goals, especially if teams outside of development will have access to the SRS

sections.title: Definitions and Acronyms
sections.text_preview: Include any non-trivial definition or acronym used in the document.

sections.title: Overall Description
sections.text_preview:
Describe what you’re going to build. Is it an update to an existing product? Is it a new product? Is it an add-on to a product you’ve already created?

These are important to describe upfront, so ever

sections.title: User classes
sections.text_preview: User classes and characteristics are critical. You’ll need to define who (different roles) is going to use the product and how. Don't forget to include each user needs.

sections.title: Assumptions and Dependencies
sections.text_preview:
There might be factors that impact your ability to fulfill the requirements outlined in this document. What are those factors?

Are there any assumptions you’re making that could turn out to be false?

sections.title: System Features and Requirements
sections.text_preview: This is where you detail the specific requirements for building your product.

sections.title: Functional Requirements
sections.text_preview:
The functional requirements describe the services and functions of a system. Functional requirements must be precise and unambiguous.

Include user stories, which are short descriptions of a feature,

sections.title: External Interface Requirements
sections.text_preview:
External interface requirements are types of functional requirements. They outline how your product will interface with other components or systems.

There are several types of interfaces you may have

sections.title: Non-functional Requirements
sections.text_preview: Non-functional requirements are restrictions on the system or the development process. Non-functional requirements can be more critical than functional ones. If they are not met, the system is useless

sections.title: Screens
sections.text_preview: Identifying the individual screens (for an app), or pages (for a website) are where a product’s shape starts to become clear. They are a distillation of the user stories into a set of distinct section

sections.title: Wireframes
sections.text_preview:
Wireframes are simple page layouts that outline the size and placement of elements, and features on a page. They are generally devoid of color, font styles, logos or any design elements.
